Epidemiology & Risk Factors.title: Prostate Cancer Epidemiology and Screening
Epidemiology & Risk Factors.html:
Prostate cancer is the single most common cancer diagnosed in American men, yet the great majority of men who have it never feel a symptom from it. Because it is usually silent, almost everything about how it is found, and the controversy around whether to look for it at all, revolves around a blood test called PSA.

How Common Is Prostate Cancer?

Prostate cancer is the most common malignancy in US men other than non-melanoma skin cancers, with a lifetime risk of about 1 in 8 men. It is also the 2nd most common cause of cancer death in men, behind only lung cancer. These two facts together explain why prostate cancer occupies so much space in oncology practice: it is extremely common, but for most men it is not the disease that ultimately kills them, many prostate cancers are slow-growing and never become life-threatening. This tension between "very common" and "often indolent" is the central theme running through screening, risk stratification, and treatment selection for this disease.

Clinical Presentation: Usually Silent

Localized prostate cancer is typically asymptomatic. When symptoms do occur, they most often reflect the tumor's effect on the urethra or bladder outlet and overlap heavily with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), a far more common non-cancerous condition:

  • Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), frequency, urgency, nocturia, and hesitancy, from bladder outlet obstruction.
  • Hematuria (blood in the urine) or hematospermia (blood in the semen), which are less common presenting signs.

Because these symptoms are nonspecific and just as likely (or more likely) to represent BPH or prostatitis, most prostate cancer today is not diagnosed because a patient complains of symptoms, it is diagnosed because a PSA test came back abnormal.

PSA Screening: Weighing Benefit Against Harm

Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is a protein produced by prostate tissue that leaks into the bloodstream at higher levels when the prostate is enlarged, inflamed, or cancerous. Screening asymptomatic men with PSA has been studied extensively in randomized trials and meta-analyses, and the results are more nuanced than "screening saves lives":

  • Screening has shown no clear decrease in overall mortality.
  • Screening does appear to reduce the incidence of distant-stage (metastatic) prostate cancer at diagnosis, based on data from the ERSPC trial.

This gap, fewer men presenting with metastatic disease, but no proven drop in overall deaths, is the crux of the screening debate. The harms of screening are real: over-diagnosis and over-treatment of cancers that would never have caused problems, complications from prostate biopsy, the downstream risks of treatment itself (incontinence, erectile dysfunction, bowel toxicity, covered in the treatment sections), and simple anxiety generated by an abnormal result. Because of this balance of modest benefit and real harms, current guidance favors shared decision-making for most men rather than a blanket "screen everyone" or "screen no one" policy.

AgeAUA screening recommendation
<40 yearsAgainst routine screening
40–54 yearsScreen higher-risk patients only (Black race, family history of prostate cancer)
55–69 yearsShared decision-making: the core screening population
>70 years with life expectancy <10–15 yearsDo not screen

Interpreting an Elevated PSA

A single PSA value is genuinely hard to interpret in isolation. A value above roughly 2.5–4 ng/mL raises concern, but the "normal" cutoff varies by age and ethnicity, and PSA can be falsely elevated by many benign causes: recent prostate manipulation or biopsy, BPH, prostatitis, urinary retention, trauma, or even recent ejaculation. Because of this, clinicians often use refinements of the raw PSA value rather than a single number:

  • PSA density (serum PSA ÷ prostate volume on imaging): >0.15 ng/mL² suggests higher cancer risk, it corrects for the fact that a larger, benign gland naturally produces more PSA.
  • PSA velocity (rate of change over time): >0.75 ng/mL/year suggests higher risk.
  • PSA doubling time: <12 months suggests higher risk (also used later, after treatment, to judge how aggressively a recurrence is behaving).
  • PSA ratio (free PSA ÷ total PSA): a ratio <25% suggests higher risk, cancer tends to produce more of the "bound" form of PSA, lowering the free fraction.
Clinical PearlNever anchor on one PSA value. A PSA of 6 ng/mL in a 45-year-old with a small, non-tender gland is far more concerning than the same value in a 75-year-old with a large, benign-feeling prostate, context (age, gland size, trend over time, recent instrumentation) is everything.
Clinical PearlThe screening data is often summarized as: PSA screening reduces the chance of being diagnosed with metastatic disease, but has not been shown to reduce the chance of dying of prostate cancer overall, which is exactly why shared decision-making, not a universal mandate, is the guideline-recommended approach for most average-risk men.

Risk Stratification & Staging.title: NCCN Risk Groups and Prostate Cancer Staging
Risk Stratification & Staging.html:
Before choosing a treatment, every man newly diagnosed with prostate cancer is sorted into a risk group. This single classification step is the hinge on which almost every later decision turns, whether active surveillance is reasonable, how much radiation dose is needed, how long hormone therapy should last, and whether additional pills or pelvic radiation should be added. Risk stratification rests on three relatively simple inputs: how far the tumor has grown (T-stage), how high the PSA is, and how aggressive the cancer looks under the microscope (Grade Group).

The Three Pillars of Risk Stratification

NCCN risk grouping is built from three variables, each reflecting a different dimension of the cancer: clinical T-stage (anatomic extent on exam/imaging), PSA (a rough surrogate for tumor burden), and Grade Group (biological aggressiveness on biopsy). No single variable is sufficient on its own, a low PSA with an aggressive Grade Group, or a modest T-stage with a very high PSA, can each independently push a patient into a higher risk category.

Understanding Gleason Score and Grade Groups

The Gleason grading system is based entirely on the architectural pattern of the cancer glands under the microscope, not on individual cell features. A pathologist identifies the primary (most common) growth pattern and the secondary (second most common) growth pattern present in the tumor, each scored on a scale from 3 (well-formed glands) to 5 (sheets of cells with no gland formation), and adds them together to produce the Gleason score (e.g., 3+4=7).

Because a Gleason sum alone can be confusing, a 3+4=7 and a 4+3=7 have the same total but very different biology, pathology reporting now also assigns a simplified Grade Group (GG) from 1 to 5. The key insight is that the order of the two numbers matters: the primary (first, dominant) pattern carries more weight than the secondary pattern. A tumor that is mostly well-formed glands with a minor component of poorly-formed glands behaves better than a tumor that is mostly poorly-formed with only a minor well-formed component, even though the Gleason sum is identical.

Grade GroupGleason scoreRisk category
GG1≤6 (3+3)Very low or low risk
GG23+4=7 (primary pattern 3)Intermediate, favorable
GG34+3=7 (primary pattern 4)Intermediate, unfavorable
GG48 (4+4, or 3+5, or 5+3)High risk
GG59–10 (4+5, 5+4, or 5+5)High or very high risk

Clinical and Pathologic T-Staging

T-stage describes the local extent of the primary tumor. T1 disease is not palpable on digital rectal exam and confined to the prostate (T1a/T1b are found incidentally on pathology from a procedure like TURP, involving <5% or >5% of the specimen respectively; T1c is found on biopsy prompted by an abnormal PSA). T2 disease is palpable but still confined to the prostate, subdivided by how much of the gland is involved (T2a: half of one side or less; T2b: more than half of one side; T2c: both sides). T3 disease has grown outside the prostate capsule (T3a: extraprostatic extension; T3b: invasion into the seminal vesicles). T4 disease has invaded fixed adjacent structures, the rectum, bladder, pelvic wall, or sphincter. Note that pathologic T-staging has no T1 category at all, since pathologic staging only applies after the prostate has been surgically removed and examined.

Putting It Together: The Six NCCN Risk Groups

Combining T-stage, PSA, and Grade Group yields six risk groups, ranging from very low risk (essentially "watch and wait" territory) to very high risk (requiring the most aggressive combined therapy):

Risk groupDefinition
Very lowT1c, GG1, PSA <10; <3 positive biopsy cores (each <50% involved)
LowT2a, GG1, PSA <10
Favorable intermediateExactly ONE intermediate factor (T2b–T2c, GG2, or PSA 10–20) AND <50% of cores positive
Unfavorable intermediateGG3, or more than one intermediate risk factor
HighT3a, GG4, GG5, or PSA >20
Very highT3b–T4, primary Gleason pattern 5, >4 cores with GG4–5, or >1 high-risk factor

Nodal and Metastatic Staging

N1 disease means regional lymph node metastasis (internal/external iliac, obturator, or presacral nodes), critically, any nodal involvement automatically makes a patient Stage IVA, regardless of how favorable the T-stage or Grade Group might otherwise look. For distant metastasis, M1a denotes nonregional lymph nodes, M1b denotes bone metastases (the most common site), and M1c denotes other visceral sites.

Genomic Classifiers as Emerging Adjuncts

Tools like the Decipher genomic classifier (a 22-gene signature scored 0–1) and the Artera AI multimodal model add a layer of biological information beyond T-stage/PSA/Grade Group. Decipher is validated as a prognostic tool, for example, in intermediate-risk patients, a low score (<0.45) carries roughly a 5% 10-year distant metastasis rate versus roughly 26% for an intermediate-high score (≥0.45). Ongoing randomized trials (NRG-GU009, NRG-GU010) are testing whether these scores can be used predictively to safely escalate or de-escalate ADT.

Clinical PearlGG2 (3+4=7) and GG3 (4+3=7) share the same Gleason sum but land in different risk categories, favorable vs. unfavorable intermediate risk, because the dominant (primary) pattern is what matters biologically. Always ask which pattern is listed first.
Clinical PearlNodal disease (N1) automatically makes a patient Stage IVA prostate cancer, no matter how favorable the T-stage or grade otherwise appears, nodal status trumps local staging in the overall stage grouping.

Imaging.title: Imaging Prostate Cancer: MRI, Bone Scan, and PSMA PET
Imaging.html:
Imaging plays two very different roles in prostate cancer care: multiparametric MRI is used to find and characterize a tumor inside the gland (and to guide biopsy), while bone scan and PSMA PET are used to look for disease that has already spread beyond the prostate and pelvis. Understanding the gland's internal anatomy is the key to interpreting all of these studies correctly.

Prostate Zonal Anatomy: Why Location Matters

The prostate is not a uniform blob of tissue, it is organized into distinct zones, and where a cancer arises strongly influences how it looks on imaging and how it is staged. Roughly two-thirds of the gland is glandular tissue (the central zone, transition zone, and peripheral zone), while the remaining third is non-glandular anterior fibromuscular stroma. The transition zone (TZ) surrounds the urethra and is where benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) arises; it also harbors 20-30% of cancers. The peripheral zone (PZ) makes up the bulk of the outer gland, classically nearest the rectum, and is where the majority (70-80%) of cancers arise, which is exactly why the peripheral zone is what a digital rectal exam is feeling for.

Multiparametric MRI: Reading Each Sequence

NCCN strongly recommends that MRI precede biopsy so that suspicious areas can be targeted directly. A multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) must include at least a T2-weighted sequence plus one additional (functional) sequence:

SequenceWhat it shows
T1-weightedHemorrhage within the prostate/seminal vesicles; enlarged lymph nodes
T2-weightedProstate volume and zonal anatomy; primary sequence for TZ lesions and for assessing extraprostatic extension/seminal vesicle invasion. A focal, circumscribed, moderately hypointense (low-signal) lesion is suspicious.
DWI/ADC (diffusion-weighted)Cancer cells are densely packed and restrict water diffusion, producing high signal on high b-value DWI with a corresponding low signal (dark) on the ADC map. This is the dominant sequence for peripheral zone lesions.
DCE (dynamic contrast enhancement)An adjunct/tie-breaker sequence only, most useful in the post-prostatectomy setting, where a new enhancing focus suggests recurrent cancer.

PI-RADS: Standardizing MRI Suspicion

The Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) assigns each lesion a score from 1 (very low suspicion) to 5 (very high suspicion) for clinically significant cancer. Critically, which sequence drives the score depends on the zone: in the peripheral zone, DWI/ADC is the dominant sequence, with DCE only able to upgrade an equivocal score of 3 to a 4 if there is focal early enhancement; in the transition zone, T2-weighted morphology is dominant, with DWI playing a secondary role.

Local Staging on MRI: Extraprostatic Extension and Seminal Vesicle Invasion

MRI is also used to assess local (T-stage) extent, distinguishing organ-confined disease (T2) from extraprostatic extension (T3a) and seminal vesicle invasion (T3b). Signs of extraprostatic extension (ECE) include capsular bulge or irregularity, obliteration of the rectoprostatic angle, direct tumor-capsule contact greater than 1.5 cm, and neurovascular bundle asymmetry. Signs of seminal vesicle invasion (SVI) include low-T2 signal replacing the normal high-T2 seminal vesicle architecture, direct extension of tumor from the prostate base, and restricted diffusion within the vesicle itself.

Staging Distant Disease: Bone Scan and PSMA PET

For unfavorable intermediate-risk or higher disease, imaging is used to rule out metastatic spread before committing to local therapy. A Tc-99m bone scan detects osseous metastases, which in prostate cancer are classically osteoblastic and appear as focal "hot spots" of tracer uptake, often in the axial skeleton (spine, pelvis, ribs). A key pitfall is the "superscan": diffusely increased skeletal uptake with faint or absent renal excretion that can be mistaken for a normal, exceptionally clean scan, when in fact it reflects such extensive, uniform osseous metastatic burden that no single "hot spot" stands out. This pattern is classically caused by prostate cancer.

PSMA PET/CT has substantially higher sensitivity than conventional imaging (CT plus bone scan) for detecting nodal and distant metastases, particularly at low PSA values during a biochemical recurrence workup, and frequently changes management. The proPSMA study demonstrated 27% better accuracy for detecting nodal or distant metastases compared to conventional CT (92% vs. 65%, p<0.0001). PSMA tracer uptake is seen in the intraprostatic primary tumor as well as nodal, osseous, and visceral disease, but readers must recognize normal physiologic uptake in the salivary and lacrimal glands, liver, spleen, kidneys, proximal small bowel, and ganglia, which can mimic disease if misinterpreted.

Clinical PearlA bone scan "superscan" can look deceptively reassuring, the absence of a focal hot spot does NOT mean the absence of metastatic disease. Diffusely increased uptake with faint renal excretion should raise suspicion for extensive osseous tumor burden, not be read as a normal study.
Clinical PearlDCE is never the primary driver of a PI-RADS score, it is strictly a tie-breaker that can push a peripheral zone score of 3 up to a 4. If you're relying on DCE to explain a score of 5, something is off.

Treatment Paradigms: Localized Disease.title: Treating Localized Prostate Cancer
Treatment Paradigms: Localized Disease.html:
Once a man's prostate cancer has been risk-stratified, treatment intensity is matched to that risk group: very-low-risk disease may need nothing more than watchful monitoring, while very-high-risk disease is treated with combined radiation, prolonged hormone therapy, and sometimes an additional oral agent. This section walks through the treatment building blocks, active surveillance, radiation dose/fractionation, brachytherapy, and androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT), and how they are assembled by risk group.

Active Surveillance vs. Immediate Treatment

  • Low-risk disease → active surveillance (periodic PSA monitoring, treat later if disease progresses) is a reasonable default; the ProtecT trial showed ~1% prostate cancer-specific mortality, not significantly different across active monitoring, surgery, or radiotherapy + short-term ADT
  • Progression on surveillance, or patient anxiety/preference → radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy + short-term ADT; by 10 years, 55% of the ProtecT active-monitoring group had eventually received radical therapy

Toxicity signatures differ by strategy: surgery causes the worst long-term sexual/urinary function; radiation causes urinary and bowel symptoms that peak around 6 months then substantially recover; active monitoring preserves function best in the short term, though sexual function still declines gradually over time in every group.

Why Fractionation Matters: The Radiobiology of Prostate Cancer

The α/β ratio describes the dose at which the "linear" component of cell killing (from a single DNA hit) equals the "quadratic" component (from two DNA hits). Tissues with a high α/β ratio (most rapidly-dividing tumors, ~10) are relatively insensitive to changes in dose-per-fraction, while tissues with a low α/β ratio (most normal, slowly-dividing tissues, ~3) are more sensitive to it. Prostate cancer is unusual: its estimated α/β ratio is only about 1.5–3, as low as, or lower than, the surrounding normal tissue. This is the radiobiological rationale for both dose escalation at conventional fractionation and hypofractionation (fewer, larger fractions), which should preferentially damage the tumor given the similar low α/β ratios.

Definitive EBRT: Dose and Fractionation Options

Randomized trials have validated three broad fractionation strategies, all safe and effective when matched to the appropriate risk group:

StrategyRegimenKey trial(s)
Conventional fractionation (dose-escalated)~78-79.2 Gy / ~39-44 FxMultiple RCTs showed dose escalation improves biochemical control (not OS) vs. lower doses
Moderate hypofractionation70 Gy/28 Fx; 60 Gy/20 FxRTOG 0415 (low risk); PROFIT, CHHiP (intermediate risk), non-inferior biochemical control
Ultra-hypofractionation (SBRT)36.25 Gy/5 Fx; 42.7 Gy/7 FxPACE-B (low/intermediate risk); HYPO-RT-PC (intermediate/high risk), non-inferior with more acute toxicity, equalizing by 5 years
  • Higher-risk disease with an MRI-visible tumor → consider a focal simultaneous integrated boost instead of escalating the whole-prostate dose (FLAME trial: 77 Gy/35 Fx whole prostate with SIB to 95 Gy to the visible tumor; improved 5-year biochemical DFS 92% vs. 85%, no increase in late GU/GI toxicity)

Brachytherapy: Boost and Monotherapy

  • Intermediate/high-risk, boost after pelvic EBRT → LDR brachytherapy boost, 115 Gy I-125, after 46 Gy/23 Fx pelvic EBRT (ASCENDE-RT: 15-year biochemical PFS 80% vs. 53% for dose-escalated EBRT alone, but worse grade 3+ GU toxicity 18% vs. 5%, no OS difference)
  • Favorable intermediate-risk, monotherapy → LDR brachytherapy alone, non-inferior to combined EBRT + LDR (5-year PFS 83% vs. 86%) with significantly less toxicity (RTOG 0232)

Adding ADT by Risk Group, and Elective Pelvic Nodal RT

Risk groupADT
Low / favorable intermediateNone (monotherapy with RT or surgery, or active surveillance)
Unfavorable intermediateShort-term ADT, 4-6 months
HighLong-term ADT, 18-24 (up to 36) months, often with pelvic RT
Very high / node-positiveLong-term ADT + abiraterone/prednisone for 2 years, with pelvic RT
  • High estimated nodal risk by Roach formula (LN risk = [PSA × 2/3] + [(Gleason score − 6) × 10], ≥20%) → add elective whole-pelvis RT to prostate-only RT (POP-RT: improved 5-year biochemical failure-free, disease-free, and distant metastasis-free survival, not overall survival; more late grade 2+ GU toxicity)
Clinical Pearl ProtecT's headline finding, prostate cancer-specific mortality around 1% regardless of treatment strategy, applies to a mostly low-risk population. It supports active surveillance as a safe option for appropriately selected low-risk men, but should not be over-generalized to higher-risk disease, where the same trial did show more progression and metastasis with a watch-and-wait approach.
Clinical Pearl Brachytherapy boost (ASCENDE-RT) and focal EBRT boost (FLAME) both intensify dose and both improve biochemical control, but they are not interchangeable in toxicity: the brachy boost carries a substantially higher risk of grade 3+ GU toxicity, an important discussion point with patients.

Treatment Paradigms: Post-op & Metastati.title: Post-Prostatectomy and Metastatic Prostate Cancer Management
Treatment Paradigms: Post-op & Metastati.html:
Not every man's prostate cancer story ends with initial treatment. Some men recur after surgery, and some present with disease that has already spread. This section covers two distinct clinical scenarios: managing a rising PSA after radical prostatectomy, and treating cancer that has spread beyond the prostate and pelvis.

Defining Biochemical Recurrence

  • After prostatectomy → biochemical recurrence (AUA) = PSA >0.2 ng/mL on 2 consecutive readings (some clinicians also act on 2 consecutive rises >0.1 ng/mL with ultrasensitive assays)
  • After radiotherapy → biochemical recurrence (Phoenix criteria) = a PSA rise of ≥2 ng/mL above the post-treatment nadir (the prostate is still present, so PSA falls to a nadir rather than becoming undetectable)

From Adjuvant to Salvage: A Paradigm Shift

  • Positive surgical margin or pT3–T4 disease (historical approach) → immediate adjuvant RT before PSA ever becomes detectable (SWOG 8794, EORTC 22911, ARO 96-02: each showed improved biochemical PFS; SWOG 8794 also showed improved distant metastasis-free and overall survival)
  • Same risk features, modern default → wait, and treat with early salvage RT once PSA becomes detectable and rising; RAVES, RADICALS-RT, GETUG-AFU 17, and the pooled ARTISTIC meta-analysis found no difference in biochemical/event-free survival vs. immediate adjuvant RT, and salvage spares roughly half of men from ever needing radiation at all
  • Node-positive (pN1) disease → adjuvant RT remains preferred (retrospective data show an all-cause mortality benefit over salvage RT, growing with the number of positive nodes, especially ≥4)

Enhancing Salvage RT: Adding ADT and Pelvic Nodal RT

  • Pre-salvage PSA >0.6 ng/mL → add 2 years of bicalutamide to salvage RT (RTOG 9601: improved 12-year OS, 76% vs. 71%)
  • Pre-salvage PSA ≤0.6 ng/mL → no OS benefit from 2-year ADT, with a signal for increased other-cause (e.g., cardiac) mortality; avoid reflexively adding it this early
  • Shorter ADT option → 6 months of ADT with salvage RT improves 10-year biochemical PFS and distant metastasis-free survival (GETUG-AFU 16)
  • Predominantly high-risk population → 24 months of ADT improves 10-year DMFS over 6 months, 78% vs. 72% (RADICALS-HD); predominantly intermediate-risk population saw no added DMFS benefit from 6 months
  • Salvage RT, especially PSA >0.35 → add pelvic lymph node RT + short-term ADT to prostate bed RT (SPPORT/RTOG 0534: improved 5-year biochemical PFS and distant metastasis, at the cost of more blood/marrow toxicity)
  • Salvage RT dose → 64 Gy to the prostate fossa is sufficient; dose-escalating to 70 Gy showed no added benefit (SAKK 09/10) unless there is gross residual/recurrent disease

Metastatic Disease: Volume Defines the Treatment Backbone

  • mCSPC (castrate-sensitive), low-volume (≤3 bone metastases confined to vertebral bodies/pelvis, no visceral mets) → doublet therapy (ADT + abiraterone, apalutamide, or enzalutamide) + prostate-directed RT (overall survival benefit: STAMPEDE, confirmed in the STOPCAP meta-analysis)
  • mCSPC, high-volume (≥4 bone lesions with at least one outside the vertebral bodies/pelvis, or any visceral metastases) → triplet therapy (ADT + docetaxel + abiraterone or darolutamide); prostate RT has not shown the same OS benefit here
  • mCRPC → castrate-resistant despite adequately suppressed testosterone (<50 ng/dL)

Oligometastatic Disease and Radiopharmaceuticals

  • Oligometastatic disease (generally up to 5 lesions) → metastasis-directed therapy (SBRT or surgery to each visible site); improves progression-free survival, delays need to start/resume ADT (STOMP, ORIOLE)
  • mCRPC, bone-only metastases → radium-223 (Xofigo), overall survival benefit
  • mCRPC, PSMA-positive metastases (bone and/or visceral) → lutetium-177-PSMA-617 (Pluvicto), overall survival benefit
Clinical Pearl Salvage RT spares roughly half of men from ever needing postoperative radiation at all, with no penalty in biochemical outcomes compared to giving everyone adjuvant RT, but node-positive disease is the key exception where adjuvant RT still shows an outcomes benefit.
Clinical Pearl The RTOG 9601 secondary analysis is a classic "know the nuance" trial: 2 years of ADT with salvage RT clearly helps at PSA >0.6, but at PSA ≤0.6 there was no OS benefit and a signal of harm, a reminder that "more therapy is always better" is not a safe assumption.

High-Yield Literature.title: Practice-Changing Prostate Cancer Trials
High-Yield Literature.html:
Radiation oncology practice is built on landmark trials, and knowing not just what each one found but why it was designed and what it changed in practice is what separates rote memorization from real understanding. This section groups the highest-yield prostate cancer trials by the practice question each one was built to answer.

The Fractionation Revolution: Can Treatment Be Shortened?

Because prostate cancer has an unusually low α/β ratio, radiobiologists predicted it should respond at least as well, possibly better, to larger doses per fraction than a conventional 2 Gy/day schedule, while potentially sparing normal tissue no better or worse than the tumor. A series of trials tested this prediction directly against conventional fractionation. CHHiP and PROFIT each validated 60 Gy/20 Fx (moderate hypofractionation) as non-inferior to conventional dosing (74-78 Gy) for biochemical control in mostly intermediate-risk disease, while CHHiP additionally showed that pushing fractionation further, to 57 Gy/19 Fx, was not non-inferior, establishing a real floor below which hypofractionation stops being safe. PACE-B and HYPO-RT-PC pushed further still into ultra-hypofractionation (SBRT), 36.25 Gy/5 Fx and 42.7 Gy/7 Fx respectively, and found non-inferior biochemical/failure-free survival, at the cost of more acute GU/GI toxicity that mostly equalized with longer follow-up. Together, these trials moved moderate hypofractionation into standard practice and established SBRT as a legitimate option for low-to-intermediate risk disease, letting many men complete curative radiation in one to four weeks instead of eight.

Pushing the Dose: FLAME and ASCENDE-RT

A parallel line of research asked whether concentrating more dose specifically into the visible tumor (rather than uniformly escalating the whole gland's dose) could improve outcomes without added toxicity. FLAME delivered an MRI-guided simultaneous integrated boost of up to 95 Gy to the intraprostatic tumor on top of a standard 77 Gy/35 Fx course, using an "isotoxic" planning strategy that protected organs at risk even when that meant under-dosing part of the boost volume, and still improved 5-year biochemical DFS (92% vs. 85%) with no increase in late toxicity, showing that a clever planning strategy can let you have dose escalation without paying a toxicity price. ASCENDE-RT tested a different way to intensify dose, a brachytherapy boost rather than an EBRT boost, and found a much larger biochemical benefit (15-year bPFS 80% vs. 53%) but a real toxicity cost (grade 3+ GU toxicity 18% vs. 5%, including urethral stricture). Read together, these two trials teach an important lesson: dose intensification for higher-risk prostate cancer clearly works, but the toxicity profile of how you deliver that extra dose (a tightly-conformed EBRT boost vs. a brachytherapy implant) matters as much as the fact that you delivered it.

From Adjuvant to Salvage: Rewriting Post-op Radiation

An earlier generation of trials (SWOG 8794, EORTC 22911, ARO 96-02) established that adjuvant RT, given immediately after surgery to men with a positive margin or pT3 disease, improved biochemical control compared to observation, and this became the standard of care. But those trials treated everyone with these risk features, even men who might never have recurred at all. A newer generation of trials, RAVES, RADICALS-RT, and GETUG-AFU 17: asked whether waiting for early signs of biochemical recurrence (salvage RT) worked just as well, and found equivalent outcomes while sparing roughly half of men from ever needing radiation. This is a textbook example of how oncology practice evolves: an initial generation of trials proves a therapy works, and a later generation asks whether it needs to be given to everyone, or only to those who actually show signs of needing it. RTOG 9601 added a further layer of nuance to the salvage strategy itself: adding 2 years of ADT to salvage RT improved overall survival, but a secondary analysis showed this benefit was concentrated in men with a pre-salvage PSA above 0.6 ng/mL, with no benefit (and possible harm) below that threshold, reinforcing that even within an established paradigm, patient selection still matters.

Metastatic Disease: Local and Systemic Therapy Both Matter

For decades, once prostate cancer was known to have spread, treating the primary tumor itself was considered pointless, the disease was assumed to be a systemic problem requiring only systemic therapy. STAMPEDE (and the confirmatory STOPCAP meta-analysis) overturned part of that assumption: adding prostate-directed RT (55 Gy/20 Fx or 36 Gy/6 Fx) to standard ADT-based therapy improved overall survival in men with newly diagnosed, low-volume metastatic disease (5-year OS 65% vs. 53%), though not in high-volume disease. PEACE-1 built on this in the modern era of intensified systemic therapy, showing that adding prostate RT on top of ADT plus abiraterone improved radiographic PFS in low-volume disease and improved time to castration resistance across the whole population, even without a proven OS benefit. In parallel, the same STAMPEDE platform showed that adding 2 years of abiraterone/prednisolone to RT plus long-term ADT improved distant metastasis-free survival, overall survival, and PFS in high-risk/very-high-risk localized disease (node-positive, or ≥2 of: T3-4, Gleason ≥8, PSA ≥40), establishing upfront treatment intensification, not just longer ADT alone, as a modern standard for the highest-risk patients.

Radiopharmaceuticals: Delivering Radiation Through the Bloodstream

Two trials established a fundamentally different way to deliver radiation, not from an external machine or an implanted seed, but through the bloodstream, targeted to cancer cells wherever they are. ALSYMPCA tested radium-223 (Xofigo), an alpha-emitter that mimics calcium and is taken up by the high-turnover osteoblastic bone metastases characteristic of prostate cancer; in men with mCRPC and bone-only metastases, it improved overall survival (14.9 vs. 11.3 months) with minimal added toxicity, reflecting the very short range of alpha-particle radiation, which spares surrounding marrow. VISION tested lutetium-177-PSMA-617 (Pluvicto), a beta-emitter chemically linked to a molecule that binds PSMA (a protein highly expressed on prostate cancer cells); in men with PSMA-PET-positive mCRPC, including those with visceral disease, where Ra-223 has no role, it improved overall survival (15.3 vs. 11.3 months) and PFS when added to standard of care. Together, these two trials established radiopharmaceutical therapy as a distinct, non-overlapping option depending on where disease is located: Ra-223 for bone-only disease, Lu-177-PSMA-617 for disease anywhere PSMA is expressed.

Clinical PearlSTAMPEDE overturned the old assumption that treating the primary tumor is futile once cancer has spread, but only for low-volume metastatic disease. Don't over-extend this OS benefit to high-volume disease, where it hasn't been shown.
Clinical PearlThe adjuvant-to-salvage story in post-prostatectomy RT is a model for how practice evolves in oncology generally: proving a treatment works is only the first step; the next generation of trials asks who actually needs it.
Clinical PearlMatch the radiopharmaceutical to the disease pattern: Ra-223 is for bone-only mCRPC (short alpha-particle range, taken up by osteoblastic mets); Lu-177-PSMA-617 requires PSMA-PET positivity but can treat bone AND visceral disease.
